title: Chapter 15 — The Study Of Greek And Latin Literature Peculiarly Useful In Democratic Communities
paragraphs: What was called the People in the most democratic republics of antiquity was very different from what we mean by that term. In Athens all the citizens took part in public affairs, but there were only 20,000 citizens out of more than 350,000 inhabitants. All the rest were slaves and performed most of the duties that today belong to the lower or even the middle classes. Athens, then, with her universal suffrage, was after all nothing more than an aristocratic republic in which all the nobles had an equal right to govern. The struggle between patricians and plebeians in Rome must be seen in the same light: it was simply an internal quarrel between the elder and younger branches of the same family. All the citizens belonged, in fact, to the aristocracy and shared its character.

It should also be noted that among the ancients books were always scarce and expensive, and that great difficulties stood in the way of their publication and circulation. These conditions concentrated literary tastes and habits in a small number of men, who formed a small literary aristocracy out of the choicer spirits of the great political aristocracy. Accordingly, there is nothing to suggest that literature was ever treated as a trade among the Greeks and Romans.

These peoples, which were not only aristocracies but also highly polished and free nations, naturally imparted to their literary productions the defects and the merits that characterize the literature of aristocratic ages. Indeed, a very superficial survey of the literary remains of the ancients is enough to convince us that if those writers were sometimes lacking in variety, or in fertility of subject matter, or in boldness, vivacity, or power of generalization in their thoughts, they always showed exquisite care and skill in their details. Nothing in their works seems done hastily or at random: every line is written for the eye of the connoisseur, and every line is shaped after some conception of ideal beauty. No literature sets in bolder relief the fine qualities in which the writers of democracies are naturally deficient than does that of the ancients. No literature, therefore, ought to be more studied in democratic ages. This study is better suited than any other to counter the literary defects inherent in those ages. As for their more praiseworthy literary qualities, those will spring up on their own, without anyone needing to learn how to acquire them.

This point must be clearly understood. A particular course of study may be useful to the literature of a people without being appropriate to its social and political needs. If people insisted on teaching nothing but the literature of the dead languages in a community where everyone is habitually driven to make strenuous efforts to increase or maintain his fortune, the result would be a very polished but very dangerous race of citizens. Since their social and political condition would daily give them a sense of needs their education would never teach them to meet, they would trouble the State in the name of the Greeks and Romans, instead of enriching it by their productive work.

It is clear that in democratic communities the interest of individuals, as well as the security of the commonwealth, demands that the education of the majority be scientific, commercial, and industrial, rather than literary. Greek and Latin should not be taught in every school, but it is important that those who by natural disposition or by fortune are destined to cultivate literature, or are prepared to enjoy it, should find schools where a complete knowledge of ancient literature can be acquired and where the true scholar can be formed. A few excellent universities would do more toward this end than a vast number of poor grammar schools, where superfluous subjects, badly learned, stand in the way of sound instruction in necessary studies.

All who aspire to literary excellence in democratic nations should often refresh themselves at the springs of ancient literature: there is no more wholesome course for the mind. Not that I consider the literary productions of the ancients beyond reproach. But I believe they have certain special merits, admirably suited to counterbalance our particular defects. They are a prop on the side where we are most in danger of falling.
